analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in 1318, Curson against Da. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. In February of that same year, Mr. O'Dell sold one-half of what he owned, or a one-fourth undivided interest in the oil and the gas, to one H.C. Pearson, Jr. He delivered a deed, and the deed was duly placed of record. In the same month, H.C. Pearson, Jr. conveyed his interest, the same one-fourth undivided interest, to his mother, Cecil G. Pearson. And Mrs. Pearson was the plaintiff below and is the appellant in this case. The deed from son to mother was duly delivered and duly placed of record. This all took place in February of 1937. In 1939, the assessment came on the land books in the name of H.C. Pearson, Jr. It was never transferred over to his mother. It stayed, unfortunately, in the name of H.C. Pearson, Jr., as sometimes happens when assessors fail to pick up the second deed. However, it's... Who fails to pick it up? The assessor, the county assessor, Your Honor. It stayed on in the name of H.C. Pearson, Jr. until 1967, when it was transferred to one W.P. Dodd, who is one of the defendants in this case, one of the appellees in this court. From the time Mrs. Pearson acquired this interest, from 1938, 37, when it came on, through 1960, the taxes were properly paid, the real estate taxes. In 1961, the taxes were not paid, for reasons which we do not have a very likely oversight. In 1962, it was sold to the state by the sheriff of the county following the procedures in West Virginia. In 1964, it was certified by the state auditor to the circuit court. And in 1966, a suit was brought by the deputy commissioner of delinquent and forfeited lands for Kanawha County, West Virginia, pursuant to statute, to sell delinquent lands. This parcel was one of the parcels in that suit. It was sold to W.P. Dodd, and a deed was delivered and recorded. And that deed, of course, is the cloud that was sought to be removed when the suit was instituted in the first instance. Thereafter, Mr. Dodd ratified a former lease to which Mrs. Pearson was never a party. A well was drilled on the property, started and completed in March of 1968. And this suit was started in October of 1968 to remove the cloud on the title. And to go back just a little bit more. Starting in 1967 and continuing up to the time the well was completed, agents of Columbia Gas Transmission Corporation, which is one of the appellees here, and was the lessee in the former lease I mentioned, agents of Columbia, talked with Mrs. Pearson, talked with her husband, and with their attorney, Mr. Cullen G. Hall of Charleston, West Virginia. Obviously, in making a complete abstract of the title, as they always do before drilling a well, they ran across the full story of the tax deed and the possible outstanding interest in Mrs. Pearson. They asked Mrs. Pearson if she and her husband would enter into a lease with Columbia, the idea being, of course, that the Pearsons and the Dodds would both be lessors and Columbia would be protected. And then if any trouble developed, any title problems arose, the Pearsons and the Dodds could fight it out and Columbia would simply be a stakeholder. Mrs. Pearson refused, told Columbia, before it started drilling, that her interest was not for lease and that Columbia, if it drilled a well, would proceed at its peril. All that is in the record, I take it. Yes, Your Honor. Yes, sir. Now, I think I should say a word about the general tax proceedings for real estate property taxes in West Virginia. Up to this time, Mrs. Pearson had not asserted any claim, had she, with respect to Dodd? Yes, Your Honor. As a matter of fact, I think it's not particularly important here, but it's true she did. Her attorney took the position that the, because, and the lower court ruled against this, but that it had been forfeited because it was on in the wrong name. So he did go to the auditor and presumed to redeem the land for forfeiture for non-entry. Well, at what stage in this whole process did, was that asserted? About 1967, just about the time it's... But not in 61, 62, 63. Oh, no, Your Honor. No, Your Honor. She is an older person and didn't honestly know that her taxes had not been paid. Her husband had been paying them, I think the record shows. Yes, Your Honor. They're an older couple. He's now deceased, but at that time, he paid all the taxes. Does that record show why he stopped paying them? No, Your Honor. It does not show. There's no telling. Oversight, very likely. He didn't die at that time, really, did he? Oh, no. No, sir. He's passed away now. He was living at the time the well was drilled. It was much later that he died. Well, are you suggesting that there's something about being an older person that makes you less likely to know that your taxes ought to be paid? Yeah. Well, not necessarily, Your Honor, but perhaps it could be. These are, I won't say senile, but older. Perhaps forgetful. It happens. It could be argued the other way. You're used to it. I want to stay with it. I'm a serious one. Well, yes, Your Honor. Of course, it could be argued both ways. I'm not taking a firm stand on that. Anyway, the record doesn't tell us why it wasn't. No, sir. No, sir. It does not, Your Honor. And you represent her? Yes. Yes, Your Honor. I represent her in this court. I did not represent her in the circuit court proceeding. But in any event, there's no question of the fact that the taxes were not paid in the year 19th. No doubt about that at all, Your Honor. Incidentally, did she live in the area in which the published notice was made? She lived in Kanawha County, West Virginia, and it was published in a newspaper. We'll get to that later, but two newspapers in Charleston, West Virginia, not far away. So we don't have a situation where one lives off in California and there are published notice in West Virginia? No, sir. We have no non-resident problem here. Did his son live with Mr. and Mrs. Pearson, the appellate? Your Honor, I really don't know. I don't think he lived with them. He lived close by us. But the tax notices continued to be issued in the name of the son. Yes, Your Honor. But the father paid the taxes from 1937 until 1960. Yes, sir. So the son must have brought the tax notice to the attention of his father. Or else he went down to the courthouse and paid what was... What was recorded against the property. Yes, sir. The record does not show. I don't think it does, Your Honor. Oh, I thought the record did show that it was... I could be wrong. I could be wrong. The father and the husband was the actual person who paid the taxes. Oh, the husband paid the taxes. No doubt about that. That is the father of the son. Yes, sir. The father of the record owner. Yes, Your Honor. Yes, Your Honor. I was asking how the father happened to know. I really don't know whether he lived with his parents or not. I just don't know, sir. In the West Virginia Code, Chapter 11A has to do with enforcement of tax procedures and collection of taxes. Yes. Article 3... Forgive me. Article 3 has to do with sale of land for taxes. And that is the... It pertains to the sheriff of the county. Article 4 has to do with a suit that is brought in the circuit court for the sale of lands by the Deputy Commissioner of Delinquent and Forfeited Lands. Now, on a year after taxes become delinquent, a sheriff publishes notice in the newspaper, a delinquency notice. Then later on, in about October or November, the sheriff publishes notice again and has a sale. And it can be purchased by an individual at the sheriff's sale. That was not the case here. If it is not purchased by an individual, the sheriff declares the property sold to the state. At that time, the statute... This is the sheriff's statute. It provides for a period of 18 months from the sale to the state for redemption. Is there at that time a transfer of title, of record, recorded? No, sir. No record deed or anything like that. Just the sheriff declares it sold to the state. And... And... Yes, ma'am. Yeah, any way of records? Her deed's a record, yes, indeed. Her deed does, of course. But I'm thinking now about the tax records or any other records. No, Your Honor. No, sir. One of your positions is that she should have received notice. Unless one examined the deed book, would there have been any way for the state to have known to whom the notice should be sent? Well, we're getting... That leads me into one of my most important points, Your Honor. Well, it may be a little too near the lunch hour. Well, whatever you say, sir. Well, that's up to the Chief Justice. Shall I continue? You can continue for another minute and a half. All right, sir. I was speaking of the period of 18 months from the sale to the state for redemption, and then it was transferred to the state, certified to the circuit court, and the deputy commissioner of delinquent and forfeited lands then brings a suit in the circuit court. Now, my case in chief rests on two main points. I'll touch that. I think we'll begin there at 1 o'clock.
